questions.prompt: A view controller holds a network client, and passes a closure to it that updates self.tableView. The screen is dismissed but never deallocates. Why?
options: The table view is holding a reference to its data source.
The closure captures self strongly, the client holds the closure, and self holds the client — a cycle.
dismiss(animated:) doesn't release view controllers.
The network request is still in flight.
questions.explanation: Escaping closures capture strongly by default. [weak self] in the capture list breaks it, and then guard let self else { return } inside. The in-flight request answer is the good distractor — it delays deallocation, it doesn't prevent it, and the difference between 'late' and 'never' is what Instruments is for.

questions.prompt: You're modelling an API response that gets passed between several screens and background tasks. Struct or class, and why?
options: Class — passing structs around copies them and wastes memory.
Struct — value semantics mean no shared mutable state across threads, which is most of the concurrency bugs gone.
Class, so you can use inheritance for the different response types.
Doesn't matter — Swift optimises both the same way.
questions.explanation: Value semantics are the point: a copy can't be mutated out from under you by another queue. Swift's copy-on-write means the copying cost is mostly theoretical for the arrays and strings inside. Reach for a class when you need identity or a shared lifecycle — not by default.

questions.prompt: You're migrating a completion-handler networking layer to async/await. What does marking the view model @MainActor actually buy you?
options: It makes the network calls run on the main thread.
The compiler enforces that its state and UI updates happen on the main actor, so you stop hand-writing DispatchQueue.main.async.
It makes the class thread-safe for any access from any thread.
It's only needed for SwiftUI.
questions.explanation: @MainActor is a compile-time guarantee about where code runs, not a lock and not a threading change for the awaited work. Your awaits still suspend and the network still happens off-main; you just come back to the main actor automatically. It's the whole reason the migration is worth doing — the class of bug in the previous question stops compiling.

questions.prompt: This shipped in a client app. Where's the leak?
options: reloadData should be called on the main thread.
self is captured strongly by a closure the loader owns, and the controller owns the loader.
loader should be lazy var, not let.
onUpdate should be a delegate, not a closure.
questions.explanation: Controller → loader → closure → controller. The controller never deallocates, and on a screen users push repeatedly that's a leak per visit. [weak self] fixes it. Thread safety is worth raising as a second point — you can't tell from this snippet which queue onUpdate fires on, and 'which queue does this call back on' is a good senior question to ask out loud.

questions.prompt: This works on the simulator and crashes intermittently on device.
options: Two problems: UIKit is being touched off the main thread, and try! crashes the app on any malformed response.
dataTask should be uploadTask.
The errors are being ignored with underscores.
resume() should be called before the closure is set.
questions.explanation: URLSession calls back on a background queue, so every UIKit line here is undefined behaviour that happens to work sometimes — the worst kind of bug. And try! turns a bad server response into a crash your users see rather than an error you handle. Ignoring the error parameters is the third finding, and worth mentioning.

questions.prompt: How would you introduce Swift concurrency into a large callback-based iOS codebase without attempting a rewrite?
questions.modelAnswer: I would establish boundaries and migrate one vertical path at a time. I would wrap stable callback APIs with checked continuations, define actor or MainActor isolation at ownership boundaries, and keep Objective-C-facing interfaces compatible. Each migrated path would gain cancellation and error tests, Thread Sanitizer coverage where useful, and measurements for regressions. I would avoid Task.detached as an escape hatch and document where legacy queues still own synchronization.
keyPoints: Migrate vertical slices behind stable boundaries
Bridge callbacks carefully with checked continuations
Make actor and MainActor ownership explicit
Test cancellation, errors, and race behavior
questions.explanation: A safe concurrency migration is an interoperability plan. Explicit isolation and small boundaries let old and new models coexist while the team learns, verifies behavior, and avoids a high-risk rewrite.
